title: Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features
summary: Interpreting and controlling model behaviors through activation steering methods requires many pairs of contrastive samples that clearly exhibit desired or undesired behavior. These data pairs determine the degree to which interpretability frameworks can reliably detect model features responsible for a behavior, and therefore the ability to steer models toward or away from such behavior. In this work, we present an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for a behavior. Specifically, we show how moving beyond simple binary pairs of samples, and instead isolating samples that show degrees of features that scale linearly with behavior, allows for better disentanglement of features. We focus on detecting and steering away from sycophancy -- the tendency of language models to prioritize user validation. We demonstrate that sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, and allow for selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the desired behavior than baseline approaches. We also evaluate their ability to enable detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, and see that they either match or outperform LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines while providing lower computational demand and more interpretability guarantees. Code & Data: https://cascading-feats.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper presents an iterative data generation pipeline that uses cascading linear features to better isolate and steer model behaviors, specifically targeting sycophancy in LLMs, outperforming baselines in detection, scoring, and steering with lower computational cost and greater interpretability.
AI.motivation: Activation steering methods require high-quality contrastive data pairs to reliably detect and control model behaviors. Existing binary sample pairs are insufficient for disentangling complex features, particularly for nuanced behaviors like sycophancy.
AI.method: An iterative data generation pipeline that produces cascading samples exhibiting degrees of features scaling linearly with the target behavior (sycophancy), moving beyond binary contrastive pairs to isolate linearly separable subspaces in model activations.
AI.result: The discovered sycophancy features form linearly separable subspaces, enabling better detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering. The approach matches or outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines with lower computational demands and more interpretability guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Cascading feature isolation provides a more effective and interpretable alternative to binary contrastive samples for activation steering, with demonstrated success in detecting and mitigating sycophancy in language models.

title: Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench
summary: When a benchmark's accuracy saturates, it is often retired and replaced with a more challenging version. We show that this approach privileges accuracy and misses the opportunity to study six other key dimensions of agent performance: construct validity issues such as shortcuts, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative importance of the model versus the scaffold, and uplift from human-agent collaboration. We use CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study to demonstrate that measuring agents along these dimensions yields meaningful insights into agent performance even after accuracy saturates. First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents. We introduce an improved benchmark, CORE-Bench v1.1, and an out-of-distribution task suite, CORE-Bench OOD. Second, we find that despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. Finally, we conduct a small-scale randomized experiment to measure uplift from human-agent collaboration on real-world computational reproducibility tasks. We find a statistically significant speedup by about a factor of two -- likely underestimated due to one-fifth of human-only reproductions reaching the time limit before completing -- and describe various other findings. Together, our contributions present a more rigorous alternative to the dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that the standard accuracy-centric paradigm for evaluating benchmarks is insufficient once accuracy saturates, and proposes measuring six additional dimensions (construct validity, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold importance, and human-agent collaboration uplift). Using CORE-Bench Hard (a computational reproducibility benchmark) as a case study, the authors surface construct validity issues, introduce improved benchmarks (CORE-Bench v1.1 and CORE-Bench OOD), and demonstrate that even after accuracy saturates, meaningful insights can be gained from efficiency, reliability, and decomposition of model vs. scaffold contributions. A small-scale randomized experiment shows a statistically significant ~2x speedup from human-agent collaboration over humans alone.
AI.motivation: The current benchmark evaluation paradigm overemphasizes accuracy as the primary metric. When accuracy saturates, benchmarks are replaced rather than mined for richer dimensions of agent performance. The authors aim to demonstrate that measuring construct validity, OOD generalization, efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold decomposition, and human-agent uplift yields valuable insights even after accuracy plateaus.
AI.method: The authors use CORE-Bench Hard as a case study. They (1) identify construct validity threats (shortcuts, etc.) and release CORE-Bench v1.1 and CORE-Bench OOD to address them; (2) measure efficiency, reliability, and decompose performance contributions from model versus scaffold; (3) conduct a small-scale randomized experiment comparing human-only vs. human-agent collaborative performance on real computational reproducibility tasks.
AI.result: Despite accuracy saturation, the benchmark remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. The human-agent collaboration experiment found a statistically significant speedup of roughly 2x (likely underestimated because ~1/5 of human-only trials hit the time limit before completing). Additional findings include surface-level construct validity issues that were difficult to anticipate with less capable agents.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm should be replaced or augmented with multi-dimensional evaluation. Even after accuracy saturates, benchmarks can yield meaningful insights along dimensions like efficiency, reliability, model/scaffold decomposition, and human-agent collaboration uplift. The authors present this as a more rigorous alternative for evaluating agent performance.

title: Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models
comment: Accepted to the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability workshop
summary: Linear directions in activation space have been identified for both refusal and persona traits in instruction-tuned chat models, but the two have been studied as separate mechanisms. We show they interact: a compliant persona gates refusal. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction and intervene on both. Compliant persona steering suppresses refusal -- in Llama, the refusal rate falls from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores it to baseline; projecting out a random direction does not. Refusal is therefore gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.

AI.tldr: Compliant persona directions gate refusal directions in chat models; steering persona suppresses refusal, and refusal is gated at late layers downstream of computation.
AI.motivation: Prior work studied refusal and persona as separate mechanisms in activation space; this paper investigates how they interact.
AI.method: Extracted compliant model-persona and refusal directions from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, then intervened via steering and projection at different layers.
AI.result: Compliant persona steering suppressed refusal (e.g., Llama refusal rate dropped from 97% to 2%). Reintroducing refusal direction partially restored refusal at late layers but not early ones. Projecting out persona direction in late layers restored refusal to baseline; a random direction did not.
AI.conclusion: Refusal is gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed; refusal depends on persona, so treating it as an isolated direction is insufficient.

title: Unsupervised Memory-Enhanced Video Transformers: Obstacle Detection for Autonomous Agricultural Rover
summary: While autonomous rovers have become indispensable to precision farming, achieving consistent operational safety remains a critical challenge. Conventional safety sensors, such as LiDAR, fail to detect obstacles positioned below the plant canopy, posing a significant risk. While camera-based supervised learning methods can detect common objects, they perform poorly when faced with obstacles that were not present in their training data. Actual unsupervised anomaly detection offers a solution by learning the normal visual patterns of an environment, but often fails for the dynamic scenes captured by a moving rover.\\ This paper introduces Video Memory Transformers for Anomaly Detection (VMTAD), a fully unsupervised method designed for real-time obstacle detection in dynamic agricultural scenes. VMTAD utilizes a transformer-driven architecture augmented with a dedicated memory module. This memory module leverages temporal context by processing encoded representations of preceding frames. This approach enables the system to effectively address the dynamic context caused by the robot's movement. The model is trained using only images that represent normal operation, requiring no data labels.\\ VMTAD was rigorously evaluated on the 'Grillion' agricultural rover. On a challenging rapeseed dataset, VMTAD achieved state-of-the-art performance, reaching a 0.973 detection and 0.997 segmentation Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. A lightweight variant provides an optimal balance of high accuracy and real-time inference (14 ms), which is critical for safety, as confirmed by our analysis of the rover's total stopping distance.

AI.tldr: VMTAD is a fully unsupervised, transformer-based method for real-time obstacle detection in agricultural rovers that uses a memory module to handle dynamic scenes, achieving state-of-the-art performance (0.973 detection AUROC, 0.997 segmentation AUROC) on rapeseed datasets with a lightweight variant running at 14 ms inference time.
AI.motivation: Autonomous rovers for precision farming lack safe obstacle detection below plant canopies, as conventional sensors (LiDAR) fail and supervised learning methods cannot handle unseen obstacles. Unsupervised anomaly detection struggles with dynamic scenes from moving rovers.
AI.method: VMTAD uses a transformer-driven architecture with a dedicated memory module that processes encoded representations of preceding frames to leverage temporal context, trained on only normal-operation images without labels.
AI.result: On a rapeseed dataset using the Grillion rover, VMTAD achieved 0.973 detection AUROC and 0.997 segmentation AUROC. A lightweight variant runs at 14 ms per inference, suitable for real-time safety given the rover's total stopping distance.
AI.conclusion: VMTAD provides effective real-time obstacle detection for dynamic agricultural scenes, addressing key safety limitations of existing methods with fully unsupervised learning and temporal context integration.

title: AlgoEvolve: LLM-driven Meta-evolution of Algorithmic Trading Programs
summary: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. Most current applications focus on static coding benchmarks. We extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading. This domain is uniquely challenging because it is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous. We present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates, evaluates, and iteratively improves executable trading strategies. These strategies are expressed as Python code and evaluated through a rigorous testing protocol. Across multiple experiments, the system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules. We further introduce a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts guiding program synthesis in the inner loop. This outer loop discovers improved search heuristics. These heuristics balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures. They consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven evolutionary framework (AlgoEvolve) for algorithmic trading that generates and iteratively improves trading strategies as Python code, with a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves prompt heuristics to outperform human-designed instructions.
AI.motivation: Extend LLM-based semantic mutation operators for evolutionary program discovery from static coding benchmarks to the challenging domain of algorithmic trading, which is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous.
AI.method: AlgoEvolve: an LLM-driven evolutionary framework where trading strategies are expressed as Python code, iteratively improved through evaluation via a rigorous testing protocol, and further enhanced by a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves prompts guiding inner-loop program synthesis.
AI.result: Emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic including autonomous shifts in trading rules; meta-evolution discovers improved search heuristics that balance exploration/exploitation and reduce zero-trade failures, consistently outperforming initial human-designed instructions.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments like algorithmic trading.

title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Autonomous Microrobot Navigation and Intervention in Simulated Blood Capillaries
summary: Autonomous microrobots navigating biological vasculature could enable targeted drug delivery and thrombolysis, yet training control policies for realistic environments remains an open challenge. Prior reinforcement learning (RL) studies of microrobotic navigation have been limited to idealized geometries that omit complex hydrodynamic flow fields, confined branching structures, and dense cellular obstacles found in vivo. Here, we develop a physically grounded simulation of a blood capillary network, incorporating realistic hydrodynamic flow fields, explicit red blood cell dynamics, and anatomically derived branching geometry, and train deep RL agents to navigate it via chemotaxis. We systematically map the physical limits of navigation across robot size and swimming speed, revealing a forbidden regime where Brownian motion and flow overcome propulsion. Successful agents independently discover multiple universal strategy types, including run-and-rotate and energy-efficient search-and-sit policies, regardless of robot parameters. Without retraining, these agents perform targeted blocking and unblocking of capillary flow, restoring throughput to healthy baseline levels. These results establish RL as a viable framework for developing autonomous microrobotic intervention strategies in complex biological environments.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a physically realistic blood capillary simulation with hydrodynamic flows, red blood cell dynamics, and branching geometry, then uses deep RL to train microrobots for navigation via chemotaxis. Agents discover universal strategies (run-and-rotate, search-and-sit) and successfully perform targeted capillary blocking/unblocking to restore healthy flow without retraining.
AI.motivation: Prior RL studies of microrobotic navigation used idealized geometries that omit complex hydrodynamic flow fields, confined branching structures, and dense cellular obstacles found in vivo, making training for realistic environments an open challenge.
AI.method: Developed a physically grounded blood capillary network simulation with realistic hydrodynamics, explicit red blood cell dynamics, and anatomically derived branching geometry; trained deep RL agents via chemotaxis.
AI.result: Systematically mapped physical limits of navigation across robot size and swimming speed, revealing a forbidden regime. Agents discovered multiple universal strategy types (run-and-rotate, energy-efficient search-and-sit). Agents performed targeted capillary blocking/unblocking, restoring throughput to healthy baseline without retraining.
AI.conclusion: RL is a viable framework for developing autonomous microrobotic intervention strategies in complex biological environments.

title: Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols
summary: As AI agent protocols proliferate, the governance structures shaping their interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined. We introduce an LLM-powered comparative pipeline for large-scale governance discourse analysis, integrating automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study socio-technical power structures at scale. We validate it on two contrasting standards for agent interoperability: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Analyzing 4,323 governance participation records, we combine LLM-assisted coding, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to examine how institutional design shapes thematic priorities and community structure. We find that while governance form influences substantive focus, both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings illustrate how LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an LLM-powered pipeline combining automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study governance structures in AI agent interoperability standards. Analyzing 4,323 records from ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led), the authors find that governance form influences thematic focus, but both regimes show similar participation inequality and fragmentation. Permissionless governance exhibits denser discourse alignment, suggesting open systems foster thematic convergence despite decentralized participation.
AI.motivation: Governance structures shaping AI agent interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined despite the proliferation of agent protocols. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing large-scale comparative analysis of socio-technical power structures in standards governance.
AI.method: The authors built an LLM-powered comparative pipeline integrating: (1) LLM-assisted automated annotation, (2) neural topic modeling, and (3) multi-layer network analysis. They applied this to 4,323 governance participation records from two contrasting standards: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led).
AI.result: Governance form influences substantive thematic focus, but both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless (ERC-8004) setting, indicating open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

title: RMTL: Reinforced Micro-task Learning for Long-Horizon Manipulation with VLM Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for robotic manipulation often requires manually designing a dense reward function, which is difficult to tune and often fragile, or learning a reward from human demonstrations or preferences, which can be expensive. A recent line of work uses pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) as zero-shot reward models, replacing these costs with a single text prompt. However, we argue that a single global prompt is too coarse for long-horizon manipulation tasks with randomized initial conditions. The single-prompt VLM reward is near-flat for much of the trajectory, making early progress hard for the agent to detect. We propose Reinforced Micro-Task Learning (RMTL), an approach that decomposes a manipulation task into a small set of language-described micro-tasks and trains the agent to switch between them. At each step, the agent receives a multi-view VLM reward computed using the prompt of the currently active micro-task and averaged across multiple camera views to reduce the effect of view-specific occlusions. A reverse curriculum gradually exposes the agent to harder initial conditions, while a PPO worker is first trained with a fixed distance-based rule that selects the active micro-task. We then replace this rule with a learned hierarchical manager, turning rule-based phase selection into a fully learned hierarchical policy. We instantiate RMTL on the Fetch manipulation environment using three short stage-specific prompts and without additional prompt tuning. Experiments show that RMTL provides more informative reward signals than single-prompt VLM rewards, enabling faster learning. These results suggest that decomposing VLM rewards into micro-task-specific language prompts can substantially improve the scalability of language-guided reinforcement learning for robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: Reinforced Micro-Task Learning (RMTL) decomposes long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks into language-described micro-tasks, each with its own multi-view VLM reward prompt, combined with a reverse curriculum and hierarchical policy to provide more informative reward signals than single-prompt VLM rewards, enabling faster reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Single-prompt VLM rewards are too coarse for long-horizon manipulation tasks with randomized initial conditions, producing near-flat reward signals that make early progress difficult for the agent to detect.
AI.method: RMTL decomposes a manipulation task into language-described micro-tasks, uses multi-view VLM rewards per active micro-task, applies reverse curriculum for harder initial conditions, trains a PPO worker with a distance-based rule for phase selection, then replaces the rule with a learned hierarchical manager.
AI.result: RMTL provides more informative reward signals than single-prompt VLM rewards, enabling faster learning on the Fetch manipulation environment without additional prompt tuning.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing VLM rewards into micro-task-specific language prompts substantially improves the scalability of language-guided reinforcement learning for robotic manipulation.

title: Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking
summary: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants. A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a multi-agent, knowledge-graph-based framework integrating 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and 20 years of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System data for nine antidepressants. Using LLM-based entity recognition (F1 up to 0.973), they find patient forums are highly concordant with each other (Jaccard up to 0.905) but diverge from FDA reports, with many adverse events appearing in community sources hundreds of days before FDA records. The Neo4j knowledge graph preserves provenance, keeping regulatory facts and patient experience distinct.
AI.motivation: Patients increasingly seek online medication information, but psychiatric drug safety knowledge is split between authoritative-but-abstract regulatory records and experience-near-but-unvalidated patient narratives. Integrating these without conflating evidence and anecdote is critical in psychiatry, where poorly contextualized information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence.
AI.method: A provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework integrating 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and 20 years of FDA FAERS data for nine antidepressants. An LLM-based entity recognition pipeline was benchmarked against physician annotations. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance.
AI.result: Entity recognition achieved highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. Patient platforms had high concordance (Jaccard up to 0.905) but diverged from FDA reports. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before FDA records.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware integration establishes a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, keeping regulatory facts distinct from patient experience, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

title: LiMoDE: Rethinking Lifelong Robot Manipulation from a Mixture-of-Dynamic-Experts Perspective
summary: Building a generalist robot that can leverage prior knowledge for continuous task adaptation remains a significant challenge. Previous works alleviate the catastrophic forgetting problem by parameter-efficient fine-tuning for single-task adaptation. However, they fail to extract reusable skills and model the interaction with other skills effectively. Recent works try to address these issues by learning prompts. Differently, this paper presents an architectural perspective on the Lifelong Mixture of Dynamic Experts (\textit{LiMoDE}), a novel two-stage learning scheme for lifelong robot manipulation. Specifically, a dynamic MoE structure is first proposed in the multi-task pre-training stage to learn prior knowledge, where a varied number of heterogeneous experts are activated based on the motion information to address different short-term manipulations. Subsequently, in the task adaptation stage, we design a lifelong MoE adaptation mechanism % (LiMoEAM) that learns lifelong experts and dynamically combines them with frozen ones for new tasks, facilitating the knowledge transfer during adaptation. The proposed \textit{LiMoDE} is evaluated on both the simulated lifelong learning benchmark and real-world tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving superior performance and strong lifelong adaptation by introducing a moderate number of additional trainable parameters and inference overhead.

AI.tldr: LiMoDE introduces a two-stage lifelong learning scheme for robot manipulation using a dynamic Mixture of Experts structure that activates heterogeneous experts based on motion information in pre-training, then combines lifelong experts with frozen ones during task adaptation to achieve superior lifelong adaptation with moderate extra parameters.
AI.motivation: Building a generalist robot that leverages prior knowledge for continuous task adaptation is challenging. Previous works suffer from catastrophic forgetting or fail to extract reusable skills and model their interactions effectively.
AI.method: (1) Multi-task pre-training stage: a dynamic MoE structure activates a varied number of heterogeneous experts based on motion information for different short-term manipulations. (2) Task adaptation stage: a lifelong MoE adaptation mechanism learns lifelong experts and dynamically combines them with frozen ones for new tasks to facilitate knowledge transfer.
AI.result: Evaluated on both simulated lifelong learning benchmarks and real-world tasks, achieving superior performance and strong lifelong adaptation with moderate additional trainable parameters and inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: LiMoDE effectively addresses lifelong robot manipulation by enabling knowledge transfer and mitigating catastrophic forgetting through a dynamic MoE architecture with a two-stage training paradigm.

title: Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System
comment: Accepted at the IEEE Conference on Games (IEEE CoG) 2026
summary: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

AI.tldr: DD-Elo enhances traditional Elo ratings by integrating move-level data using a drift diffusion model from cognitive neuroscience, enabling faster adaptation to skill changes while maintaining theoretical alignment with standard Elo.
AI.motivation: Traditional Elo rating systems suffer from response lag because they only use match outcomes and ignore granular gameplay quality. Incorporating move-by-move data is challenging due to noise and vast game-state space.
AI.method: The authors propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), which models skill expression as a decision-making process inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. This framework integrates move-level data into rating adjustments and is backed by rigorous mathematical derivation showing bounded deviation from traditional Elo.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than the traditional Elo system while maintaining theoretical alignment with it.
AI.conclusion: DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems.

title: Morphology-Specific Closed-Loop Control of Logarithmic-Spiral Continuum Arms via Online Jacobian Error Compensation
summary: Logarithmic spirals are ubiquitous in biological appendages and provide an attractive morphology for continuum manipulators capable of reaching, wrapping, and grasping. Recently reported logarithmic-spiral robots demonstrated scalable fabrication and versatile grasping but lacked inverse kinematics and closed-loop control. This work presents the first morphology-specific closed-loop task-space control framework for logarithmic-spiral continuum arms. A segmented tendon-driven model with a centerline backbone and equilateral tendon routing is developed in MuJoCo to capture tapered compliance and contact dynamics. An analytical task-space Jacobian is derived directly from the logarithmic-spiral kinematics and combined with online Jacobian error compensation using a Broyden secant update and Kalman-filter estimation. The resulting controller continuously corrects modeling errors arising from nonlinear deformation, contact, and geometric mismatch. The framework is validated through planar and spatial simulations, including trajectory tracking, attitude regulation, disturbance rejection, three-dimensional position tracking, and simultaneous position-orientation control. Compared with a piecewise-constant-curvature (PCC) baseline, the proposed method consistently reduces tracking errors, suppresses attitude drift, and maintains a bounded Jacobian estimation error. The controller is further applied to morphology-enabled manipulation tasks, including obstacle-assisted reach-wrap-release motions, adaptive whole-arm grasping, and cooperative multi-arm object handling. Results demonstrate that combining logarithmic-spiral morphology with online Jacobian compensation enables accurate, robust, and scalable control of highly underactuated continuum manipulators. The proposed framework establishes a physics-grounded baseline for future hardware implementation and learning-augmented soft robotic control.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first closed-loop task-space control framework for logarithmic-spiral continuum arms, combining analytical Jacobian derived from spiral kinematics with online error compensation (Broyden update + Kalman filter). The method outperforms PCC baselines in trajectory tracking, attitude regulation, and manipulation tasks like reach-wrap-release and cooperative grasping.
AI.motivation: Logarithmic-spiral continuum robots have demonstrated scalable fabrication and versatile grasping, but lack inverse kinematics and closed-loop control, limiting their practical utility.
AI.method: A segmented tendon-driven model in MuJoCo with centerline backbone and equilateral tendon routing; analytical task-space Jacobian from logarithmic-spiral kinematics combined with Broyden secant update and Kalman-filter-based online Jacobian error compensation.
AI.result: The proposed method consistently reduces tracking errors, suppresses attitude drift, and maintains bounded Jacobian estimation error compared to PCC baseline; validated on planar/spatial trajectory tracking, disturbance rejection, and manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining logarithmic-spiral morphology with online Jacobian compensation enables accurate, robust, and scalable control of highly underactuated continuum manipulators, providing a physics-grounded baseline for future hardware and learning-augmented control.

title: Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems
summary: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a computational governance model for AI agents where high-risk actions require independently attested evidence from authoritative sources, enforced through cryptographic verification and tamper-evident logging, rather than monitoring agent reasoning.
AI.motivation: AI agents are beginning to perform consequential, irreversible actions (e.g., clinical prescribing, software deployment), and existing approaches of monitoring agent reasoning are insufficient for governing such autonomous actors.
AI.method: The authors formalize a governance model based on human institutional patterns: agents retain autonomy over planning/reasoning but hold no execution authority over high-risk actions. Execution requires independently attested preconditions from authoritative sources, cryptographically bound to declared intent, evaluated by a deterministic policy, with tamper-evident logging for re-verification. A proof-of-concept implementation is provided.
AI.result: A computational governance model with proof-of-concept implementation, illustrated through software deployment and clinical prescribing examples.
AI.conclusion: Independent attestation at the point of action, rather than reasoning monitoring, offers a viable governance model for autonomous AI agents performing high-risk actions, enabling accountability and verifiability.

title: OmniContact: Chaining Meta-Skills via Contact Flow for Generalizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: Learning long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation poses a dual challenge: it requires not only the robust execution of meta-skills but also their seamless, closed-loop chaining equipped with autonomous recovery. Existing approaches remain limited: explicit humanoid-object interaction representations offer precision but are notoriously difficult for high-level planning, whereas implicit skill embeddings are compact but lack the interpretability required for reliable composition. We propose \ours, a hierarchical framework centered on \textbf{contact flow (CF)}, a compact representation consisting of key body trajectories and time-series binary contact signals. Leveraging this shared interface, our low-level policy \textbf{CF-Track} learns a unified library of loco-manipulation skills, while our high-level module \textbf{CF-Gen} heuristically synthesizes future contact-flow sequences. To support this setting, we additionally collect the OmniContact dataset, a MoCap-based HOI corpus for humanoid loco-manipulation (Appendix~\ref{sec:dataset}). Together, they enable robust execution, autonomous failure recovery, and flexible composition of meta-skills for long-horizon tasks. Experiments show that OmniContact achieves \(98.7\%\) success on \textit{Carry Box} and \(76.5\%\) on \textit{Push-Stack Boxes}, outperforming prior baselines by average margins of \(40.9\%\) in meta-skill and \(66.5\%\) in skill chaining. Besides, our framework naturally integrates with VLMs for semantic task decomposition, enabling complex, semantically grounded loco-manipulation behaviors, such as arranging scattered boxes into a heart shape.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical framework (OmniH2O) using contact flow representation for long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation, combining low-level skill tracking (CF-Track) with high-level contact flow synthesis (CF-Gen), achieving significant improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing humanoid loco-manipulation methods struggle with either precision (explicit HOI representations are hard for planning) or interpretability (implicit embeddings lack reliable composition), and none effectively handle long-horizon tasks requiring robust skill chaining and autonomous recovery.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical framework centered on contact flow (CF)—key body trajectories + binary contact signals. Low-level CF-Track learns unified skill library; high-level CF-Gen synthesizes future CF sequences. Also introduces OmniContact dataset (MoCap-based HOI corpus). Integrates with VLMs for semantic task decomposition.
AI.result: 98.7% success on Carry Box, 76.5% on Push-Stack Boxes; outperforms baselines by 40.9% in meta-skill and 66.5% in skill chaining on average.
AI.conclusion: The contact flow representation enables robust execution, autonomous failure recovery, flexible skill composition for long-horizon tasks, and seamless integration with VLMs for semantically grounded complex behaviors.

title: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami
summary: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

AI.tldr: COrigami is an end-to-end AI pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions, combining geometric optimization with aesthetic evaluation via reinforcement learning to enable human-AI co-creativity in computational origami.
AI.motivation: Generative AI struggles to produce physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints (e.g., flat foldability) and subjective visual aesthetics; this gap is addressed in the mathematically rigid domain of computational origami.
AI.method: The pipeline includes: (1) generating a semantic stick figure from natural language, (2) computing a base packing, (3) solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, (4) shaping the flat-folded pattern, and (5) refining via reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop.
AI.result: The system generates structural starting points that satisfy multi-objective physical constraints (flat foldability) while incorporating aesthetic quality, serving as an effective collaborative assistant for human artists.
AI.conclusion: By integrating algorithmic optimization with autonomous aesthetic critique, AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity in physical art generation.

title: RoboTales: ROBOTic Anthropomorphic LEarning Systems
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, HRI Companion '26: Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction, Student Design Challenge
summary: RoboTales is a low-cost robotic storytelling system that animates narratives using expressive sock puppetry. Implemented autonomously on a Baxter robot as a test case, RoboTales synchronizes narration, gestures, and mouth movements to perform character-driven stories. In a pilot study, puppet-based storytelling outperformed a gesture-only mode, producing higher HRIES ratings and improved story recall, suggesting that embodied puppetry enhances engagement and narrative comprehension. Designed to be modular and platform-agnostic, RoboTales can be adapted to other manipulators and offers a screen-free alternative to passive media, supporting future deployment in child-centered learning environments.

AI.tldr: RoboTales is a low-cost, autonomous robotic storytelling system that uses expressive sock puppetry on a Baxter robot. A pilot study showed puppet-based storytelling outperformed gesture-only mode in engagement and narrative recall, offering a screen-free, modular, and platform-agnostic approach for child-centered learning.
AI.motivation: To develop an engaging, screen-free alternative to passive digital media for children, leveraging embodied robotic puppetry to enhance engagement and narrative comprehension in storytelling.
AI.method: RoboTales was implemented on a Baxter robot, synchronizing narration, gestures, and mouth movements to perform character-driven stories using sock puppets. A pilot study compared puppet-based storytelling against a gesture-only mode, measuring HRIES ratings and story recall.
AI.result: Puppet-based storytelling outperformed gesture-only mode, yielding higher HRIES ratings and improved story recall, indicating enhanced engagement and narrative comprehension.
AI.conclusion: Embodied puppetry effectively enhances engagement and comprehension in robotic storytelling. The system is modular and platform-agnostic, suitable for adaptation to other manipulators and future deployment in child-centered learning environments.

title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by their first names
summary: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

AI.tldr: Verification is becoming harder than generation for coding agents; this paper characterizes verification signal quality across scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, examines four reward constructions, and shows that verification must co-evolve with generator capability as no fixed reward function remains effective.
AI.motivation: The classical intuition that verifying is easier than producing is inverted for modern coding agents: generating candidate solutions has become easier while reliably verifying them has become harder, because every verifier is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This creates a twofold difficulty: intent is inherently underspecified, and optimization widens the proxy-intent gap via reward hacking or signal saturation.
AI.method: The paper characterizes verification signal quality along three dimensions: scalability, faithfulness, and robustness. It studies four reward constructions: (1) a test verifier for general coding tasks, (2) a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, (3) the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and (4) an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Experiments are conducted across different task types and policy capability levels.
AI.result: Targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. The core observation is that no fixed reward function remains effective as policy capability grows.
AI.conclusion: Verification must co-evolve with the generator; fixed reward functions cannot remain effective as policy capability continues to improve.

title: TaskNPoint: How to Teach Your Humanoid to Hit a Backhand in Minutes
summary: How do we learn to hit a tennis backhand? Not from a thousand hours of tennis tournaments on TV - we work with a coach and practice. We argue this is also the right recipe for teaching dynamic skills to humanoid robots. This follows from a structural property of dynamic skills: the outcome is decided by a short, crucial portion of the trajectory - for a backhand, the ~20cm of racket travel around ball contact. Getting this interaction window right requires coordinating the whole motion, so that control, physics, and morphology act in concert. Learning thus reduces to mastering a handful of distinct actions and, for each, practicing until the window comes out right. To this end, we introduce TaskNPoint, a training protocol which makes the coach-learner division of labor explicit. The human coach contributes four inputs: a discrete set of skills (e.g. different shots), one demonstration per skill, identification of the interaction window, and the goal. Learning in a physically realistic simulation environment fills in each action trajectory and provides robustness to unmodeled events. Crucially, randomized target sampling during training lets a single demonstration generalize zero-shot to unseen goal locations. We test this approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid that hits forehands and backhands against balls thrown by a human, kicks incoming soccer balls, and picks and places boxes from novel locations. We find that learning is successful from short human video demonstrations and under an hour of training on a single GPU, with no per-task reward tuning.

AI.tldr: TaskNPoint trains humanoid robots on dynamic skills (tennis, soccer, pick-and-place) using short human demonstrations and under 1 hour of GPU training, by having a human coach specify discrete skills, one demo per skill, interaction windows, and goals, while the system learns full trajectories via randomized target sampling for zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Learning dynamic skills (e.g., tennis backhand) from watching videos (e.g., TV) is ineffective because the outcome depends on a short critical trajectory window (e.g., ~20cm around ball contact). Instead, the authors argue for a coach-learner paradigm analogous to human skill acquisition: a coach provides structured guidance, and the learner practices to get the interaction window right.
AI.method: TaskNPoint training protocol: (1) Human coach provides discrete skill set, one demonstration per skill, interaction window identification, and goal; (2) Learning in physically realistic simulation fills in full action trajectories; (3) Randomized target sampling during training enables zero-shot generalization to unseen goal locations from a single demonstration.
AI.result: Successfully trained a Unitree G1 humanoid to hit forehands/backhands against human-thrown balls, kick incoming soccer balls, and pick/place boxes from novel locations. Training succeeds from short human video demonstrations with under 1 hour on a single GPU, no per-task reward tuning needed.
AI.conclusion: The coach-learner paradigm (structured human guidance + targeted practice) is an effective recipe for teaching dynamic skills to humanoid robots, leveraging the structural property that skill outcomes hinge on short critical trajectory windows.

title: How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?
summary:
Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
  We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels.
  Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks, spanning data retrieval, knowledge interpretation, and quantitative modeling, with a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol and public release of artifacts.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic benchmarks cover domains like finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, but energy-domain evaluations are limited to static knowledge recall, failing to address the sector's need for live data retrieval, regulatory/market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
AI.method: The authors created 243 expert-curated problems across three categories (Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics), equipped agents with domain-specific tools (live ISO APIs, regulatory docket search, tariff databases, optimization models, RAG), and evaluated closed/open-source LLMs using a multi-dimensional protocol scoring approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity with category-aware routing.
AI.result: Comparative analysis of closed-source and open-source LLMs in terms of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional energy domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The work fills the critical gap of missing agentic benchmarks in the energy domain, demonstrating the necessity of tool-augmented LLM agents for realistic, multi-step energy market analytics tasks.

title: NavIsaacLab: Generating Realistic Crowd via Parallel Robot Learning for Benchmarking Human-aware Navigation
summary: Robot autonomous navigation that accounts for surrounding human activities is crucial for ensuring both safety and natural human-robot interaction in real-world environments shared by humans and robots. Simulation of complex and diverse navigation scenarios serves as the foundation for training reliable robot navigation policies and accurately evaluating the performance of algorithms, offering an efficient alternative to manual supervision of real data. However, current human-aware navigation research faces significant challenges due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality scene data. Existing simulation platforms often rely on handcrafted rules to approximate pedestrian behavior and lack the capability to provide extensive sensor signals, typically assuming perfect observations. To address these limitations, this paper presents NavIsaacLab, a comprehensive framework for benchmarking and training human-aware navigation policies through physics-based and photo-realistic simulations of pedestrians and scenes. Based on Isaac Lab, the proposed framework employs photo-realistic scene rendering capabilities and supports parallel simulation on GPU, delivering real-time and accurate 3D visual feedback to robots. To enhance the realism of human behavior, a data-driven approach is employed that incorporates a trajectory diffusion model and an adversarial motion learning controller, enabling controllable, physics-based pedestrian simulation. Furthermore, the integration of diverse cross-scale scenes provides a robust benchmark for state-of-the-art human-aware navigation methods.

AI.tldr: NavIsaacLab is a comprehensive framework for benchmarking and training human-aware robot navigation policies using physics-based, photo-realistic simulations with data-driven pedestrian behaviors and parallel GPU-based rendering.
AI.motivation: Current human-aware navigation research lacks diverse, high-quality scene data; existing simulation platforms rely on handcrafted pedestrian behavior rules and assume perfect observations, failing to provide extensive sensor signals.
AI.method: Built on Isaac Lab, the framework uses photo-realistic scene rendering with GPU-parallel simulation for real-time 3D visual feedback. It employs a trajectory diffusion model and adversarial motion learning controller for data-driven, physics-based pedestrian simulation, and integrates diverse cross-scale scenes.
AI.result: The framework delivers real-time, accurate 3D visual feedback to robots and provides a robust benchmark for state-of-the-art human-aware navigation methods through controllable, realistic pedestrian simulations.
AI.conclusion: NavIsaacLab addresses the scarcity of high-quality scene data and limitations of handcrafted pedestrian models, enabling more realistic training and evaluation of human-aware navigation policies.

title: What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

AI.tldr: MLLM evaluation lags behind model capabilities; existing benchmarks are task-isolated and fail to assess cross-modal integration; key gaps include temporal-spatial coherence, physical understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation benchmarks for multimodal large language models are limited to isolated tasks and do not assess whether models truly integrate information across modalities, creating a gap between capability advancement and meaningful evaluation.
AI.method: The authors examine existing evaluation means for MLLMs and review the benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps in current evaluation practices.
AI.result: Four key evaluation gaps are identified: temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention.
AI.conclusion: Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries of MLLMs.

title: Racing a Wheeled Quadruped: Active Load Transfer Mitigation via Model Predictive Control
comment: Accepted to the 17th International Symposium on Advanced Vehicle Control (AVEC 2026), 7-11 September 2026, Tsukuba, Japan
summary: This paper presents a hierarchical control framework using model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning (RL) for active roll control to manage lateral load transfer during autonomous racing of a wheeled quadruped. The framework integrates offline time-optimal raceline generation, an online MPC planner that actively minimizes the lateral Load Transfer Ratio (LTR), and a low-level, whole-body RL policy deployed directly onto the robot's 16 actuators. The MPC is based on a vehicle dynamics bicycle model of the Unitree Go2-W platform. The robot's leg actuators act as active suspension where knee joints generate anti-roll torque to bank into turns. Physical track experiments demonstrate that active roll control reduces mean LTR by up to 44%, improves the fastest lap time by 8.7%, and boosts peak lateral acceleration capability by 21.3% to 1.98 $m/s^2$, maintaining robust high-speed stability beyond the range of a non-tilting baseline controller. Supplementary code and video can be found at https://github.com/meisman-ucb/go2w-roll-control-mpc

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hierarchical control framework combining MPC and RL for active roll control in wheeled quadruped autonomous racing, achieving up to 44% reduction in lateral load transfer, 8.7% faster lap times, and 21.3% higher lateral acceleration.
AI.motivation: To improve high-speed stability and cornering performance in autonomous racing of wheeled quadrupeds by actively managing lateral load transfer through active roll control.
AI.method: A hierarchical framework with three layers: offline time-optimal raceline generation, an online MPC planner (based on a bicycle model) that minimizes the lateral Load Transfer Ratio (LTR), and a low-level whole-body RL policy deployed on 16 actuators, using leg knee joints as active suspension to generate anti-roll torque.
AI.result: Mean LTR reduced by up to 44%, fastest lap time improved by 8.7%, peak lateral acceleration increased by 21.3% to 1.98 m/s² on the Unitree Go2-W platform in physical track experiments.
AI.conclusion: Active roll control via hierarchical MPC-RL framework significantly enhances high-speed stability and cornering performance beyond non-tilting baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of using leg actuators as active suspension in wheeled quadruped racing.

title: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
summary: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train-test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training

AI.tldr: OpenFinGym is a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agents covering forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection, with automated task-construction from financial publications, containerized runtime, paper trading engine, and support for SFT/RL post-training.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of large language model agents in quantitative finance is fragmented across isolated tasks, overlooks financial relevance, and fails to capture multi-stage interdependent workflows (forecasting, strategy, risk management, trading). Single-task platforms overstate agent competence and miss weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making.
AI.method: OpenFinGym provides: (1) a unified gym environment covering forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution/verification interface; (2) an automated task-construction pipeline that converts quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; (3) containerized runtime with a host-side verifier preventing train-test leakage; (4) paper trading engine with low-latency data-stream design; (5) deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; (6) integration for SFT and RL post-training.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract (the paper introduces the platform rather than presenting experimental results).
AI.conclusion: OpenFinGym addresses fragmentation in quantitative-finance agent evaluation by providing a unified, scalable environment that supports multi-stage workflows, automated task creation from publications, and post-training integration, enabling more realistic and comprehensive assessment of agent capabilities.

title: Layered Outer-Loop Control for Disturbance-Robust Multi-Waypoint UAV Arrival
summary: Disturbance-robust UAV position control is easy to demonstrate in benign simulations but much harder to make fast in approach, well behaved near the target, and credible beyond a single benchmark. This letter presents a layered terminal-control architecture for multi-waypoint UAV position regulation together with a staged evaluation across PyBullet, PX4/Gazebo, and hardware. Phase I uses a PyBullet benchmark with stochastic wind for rapid structural selection, identifying a controller core that separates smooth approach generation, persistent-bias compensation, and supervised near-target terminal regulation. Phase II carries only that main architecture into a more demanding PX4/Gazebo closed loop, where the outer-loop controller acts through a cascaded flight stack with delay-sensitive settling and stronger transit-to-hover coupling. This step exposes which benchmark gains survive autopilot-mediated dynamics and which refinements collapse once the loop becomes more deployment-like. In Phase I, the bare controller attains 0.024 m mean late-stage wind error. In Phase II, the final controller is selected using a transfer-oriented rule emphasizing absence of benchmark priors, cross-scenario balance, and deployable supervisory logic. Strict is used as the primary reporting reference; the supplementary retrospective Grace analysis shows that part of the residual failure set is sensitive to completion semantics rather than gross waypoint-miss behaviour. The evaluation is completed on one Vicon-tracked Tello stack through a two-level hardware study. Taken together, the results suggest that benchmark success becomes more informative when the main controller design is separated from benchmark-specific refinement and remains defensible under harder closed-loop evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a layered terminal-control architecture for multi-waypoint UAV position regulation with a staged evaluation across simulation (PyBullet, PX4/Gazebo) and hardware (Vicon-tracked Tello). The architecture separates smooth approach generation, persistent-bias compensation, and supervised near-target terminal regulation. Results show 0.024 m mean late-stage wind error in PyBullet, with transfer-oriented selection rules to avoid benchmark-specific overfitting.
AI.motivation: Disturbance-robust UAV position control is easy in benign simulations but difficult to make fast, well-behaved near targets, and credible beyond a single benchmark. Existing approaches often overfit to specific simulation environments and fail under more realistic closed-loop conditions.
AI.method: A layered terminal-control architecture with three components: smooth approach generation, persistent-bias compensation, and supervised near-target terminal regulation. Staged evaluation: Phase I in PyBullet with stochastic wind for rapid structural selection; Phase II in PX4/Gazebo with cascaded flight stack, delay-sensitive settling, and transit-to-hover coupling; hardware evaluation on Vicon-tracked Tello.
AI.result: Phase I: 0.024 m mean late-stage wind error. Phase II: final controller selected via transfer-oriented rule emphasizing absence of benchmark priors, cross-scenario balance, and deployable supervisory logic. Grace analysis reveals residual failures sensitive to completion semantics rather than waypoint-miss behavior.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark success becomes more informative when the main controller design is separated from benchmark-specific refinement and remains defensible under harder closed-loop evaluation.

title: Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems
comment: 8 pages, 2 tables. Accepted to the ICML 2026 Workshop on Failure Modes in Agentic AI (FAGEN), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and formalizes compositional behavioral leakage (CBL) — a failure mode where editing one prompt module in agentic systems silently alters behavior of other modules sharing a context window — due to transformer self-attention's lack of architectural isolation. Using a 144-trial protocol on a deployed Claude Sonnet agent, they find only content-channel perturbations produce measurable interference (Cohen's d=0.63), in a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding over thousands of decisions.
AI.motivation: Practitioners observe that modifying one prompt module in agentic systems unexpectedly shifts behavior of other modules, despite no explicit dependencies. This recurring but uncharacterized failure mode threatens reliability of deployed prompt-composed agents.
AI.method: A three-channel protocol (volume, content, form) perturbing non-focal modules on a deployed Claude Sonnet 4.6 job-evaluation agent across 144 trials, measuring behavioral changes via Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Only the content channel produces detectable paired effects (Cohen's d=0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero). No recommendations flipped — effects exist in a sub-threshold regime undetectable by standard QA but cumulatively significant across large-scale deployment.
AI.conclusion: CBL is a distinct failure axis orthogonal to adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, and privacy leakage. Cross-module interference measurement should be a standard requirement for evaluating prompt-composed agent systems.

title: KRVF: A Source-Aware Semantic Voxel World Representation for Edge Mobile Manipulation
summary: Mobile manipulators need world models that are current, queryable, semantically meaningful, and usable under edge-compute constraints. This technical report presents KRVF, a source-aware semantic voxel world representation for edge mobile manipulation. Unlike reconstruction-centric mapping pipelines that primarily optimize global geometric fidelity, KRVF represents local world state as task-oriented voxels that encode occupancy, color, semantic evidence, temporal freshness, and evidence source. The representation separates measured occupancy from semantic-prior hypotheses, enabling depth-failure-aware object reasoning without silently corrupting persistent geometry. KRVF also closes a feedback loop between mapping and sensing by rendering map-prior depth for repair, and exposes task-level query operators for semantic objects and grasp candidates. The report formalizes the KRVF representation and documents a ROS 2 implementation that turns online RGB-D observations into a task-facing robot memory.

AI.tldr: KRVF is a source-aware semantic voxel world representation for edge mobile manipulators that encodes occupancy, color, semantic evidence, temporal freshness, and evidence source, enabling depth-failure-aware object reasoning and task-level queries under edge-compute constraints.
AI.motivation: Mobile manipulators require world models that are current, queryable, semantically meaningful, and usable under edge-compute constraints. Existing reconstruction-centric mapping pipelines optimize global geometric fidelity but fail to provide task-oriented representations suitable for edge deployment.
AI.method: KRVF represents local world state as task-oriented voxels encoding occupancy, color, semantic evidence, temporal freshness, and evidence source. It separates measured occupancy from semantic-prior hypotheses for depth-failure-aware reasoning, closes a feedback loop by rendering map-prior depth for repair, and exposes task-level query operators for semantic objects and grasp candidates. Implemented in ROS 2 using online RGB-D observations.
AI.result: A formalized KRVF representation and documented ROS 2 implementation that transforms online RGB-D observations into a task-facing robot memory for edge mobile manipulation.
AI.conclusion: KRVF provides a source-aware semantic voxel representation tailored for edge mobile manipulation, addressing limitations of reconstruction-centric pipelines by incorporating temporal freshness, evidence source separation, and task-level query capabilities.

title: Accelerating Returns and the Qualitative Engine for Science
summary: Ray Kurzweil described a thesis of accelerating returns, which is the most influential narratives in discussions of technological progress. Its central claim is that advances in multiple technological fields, especially compute, artificial intelligence, brain science, and biotechnology, interact in such a way that progress becomes self-amplifying and approximately exponential. This paper gives a simple mathematical interpretation of that claim and then argues that, even if such acceleration is real, it does not by itself resolve the central problem of scientific discovery. The reason is that accelerating returns apply most naturally to executional and infrastructural capability, whereas genuine discovery often depends on a different capacity: qualitative reasoning about when a current framework is structurally inadequate and what conceptual move is needed next. Recent ARC-AGI-3 results sharpen this distinction: humans solve the benchmark at ceiling, whereas frontier AI systems remain below 1%, indicating that the gap between current AI and human flexible reasoning is still very large. At the same time, Demis Hassabis has emphasized that humans must retain their sense of meaning and what they choose to focus their lives on, a reminder that the future of AI is not only a technical forecast but also a question of what forms of human understanding are worth preserving and transmitting. This paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) [3] as a response to that missing capacity. In this view, the Kurzweil theory helps explain why quantitative capability may accelerate, while QES addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone does not solve. Its value does not depend on when AGI arrives, but on the fact that the processes of scientific discovery themselves constitute a form of human wisdom worth preserving, organizing, and making accessible.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that Ray Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis explains exponential growth in quantitative/executional capability but does not resolve the core problem of scientific discovery, which requires qualitative reasoning about structural inadequacy in current frameworks. The Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) is proposed as a solution to this missing capacity, with recent ARC-AGI-3 results (human ceiling vs. AI <1%) illustrating the persistent gap.
